hypothesis: The eggNOG orthologous group ENOG410XR0J (RagB/SusD domain-containing protein) is increased/characteristic in 12-month-old infants fed dairy-based complementary protein relative to meat-fed infants.
rationale: No published study located that reports this specific eggNOG group (ENOG410XR0J) - or any individually named RagB/SusD-family gene - as differentially abundant between dairy-based and meat-based complementary feeding in infants. What the literature supports is only generic, pathway/taxon-level reasoning: RagB/SusD-family proteins are the substrate-binding lipoproteins of Bacteroidota polysaccharide utilization loci (PULs), so their metagenomic abundance largely tracks Bacteroides/Bacteroidota load and PUL repertoire, which in turn are strongly diet-responsive. The one directly relevant RCT (Tang et al., meat vs. dairy complementary foods in U.S. formula-fed infants, 5-12 mo - the same design as the group under study) reports its group-level difference for Akkermansia (increased in dairy, decreased in meat) and greater richness/butyrate increase in the meat arm; a systematic review summarizing that trial notes dairy consumption promoted longitudinal increases in Bacteroides and Clostridiales, which is weakly consistent with a dairy-side increase in Bacteroidota PUL/SusD gene content. However, this is (a) a longitudinal within-arm observation rather than a between-arm test of gene families, and (b) counterbalanced by the general diet-microbiome literature in which Bacteroides is classically associated with animal-protein/fat-rich diets, which would predict the opposite direction. The metagenomic/metabolomic analysis of this same trial (Price et al. 2025) exists in the public domain, but I could not verify from search results that it reports this RagB/SusD orthologous group or its direction. Net: relevant but indirect and partly conflicting evidence, i.e. weak support only.

evidence.title: Different gut microbiota in U.S. formula-fed infants consuming a meat vs. dairy-based complementary foods: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.study_population: Full-term, formula-fed U.S. infants randomized to meat- vs. dairy-based complementary diets from ~5 to 12 months
evidence.relevance: Only RCT directly comparing the two exposures at the 12-month timepoint; reports beta-diversity divergence at 12 months, Akkermansia increasing in the dairy arm and richness/butyrate increases in the meat arm. It does not report RagB/SusD or any eggNOG gene family, so it neither confirms nor refutes the hypothesis at the feature level.

evidence.title: The effect of complementary foods on the colonic microbiota of weaning infants: a systematic review
evidence.study_population: Systematic review of weaning-infant complementary feeding intervention studies, including the U.S. meat vs. dairy RCT
evidence.relevance: Summarizes that dairy product consumption promoted longitudinal increases in the genus Bacteroides (and Clostridiales) with decreases in Escherichia/Enterobacteriaceae - taxon-level, indirect support for higher Bacteroidota PUL (SusC/SusD-RagB) gene abundance in dairy-fed infants.

evidence.title: Network-based representation learning reveals the impact of age and diet on the gut microbial and metabolomic environment of U.S. infants in a randomized controlled feeding trial
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed infants, 5-12 months, meat vs. dairy complementary feeding RCT (fecal metagenomics + metabolomics)
evidence.relevance: Published metagenomic/metabolomic analysis of exactly this exposure and age range; establishes that diet- and age-associated metagenomic gene features are detectable, but I could not confirm from search results that ENOG410XR0J / RagB-SusD proteins are reported as dairy-associated, so it does not provide feature-specific directional support.

evidence.title: Specificity of Polysaccharide Use in Intestinal Bacteroides Species Determines Diet-Induced Microbiota Alterations
evidence.study_population: Gnotobiotic mice colonized with human gut Bacteroides species; in vitro/in vivo dietary polysaccharide switches
evidence.relevance: Establishes that susC/susD (RagB/SusD) gene pairs define PULs and that PUL content/expression determines diet-driven Bacteroides abundance shifts - the mechanistic basis for why such a gene family could differ by complementary food type, but not specific to dairy vs. meat or to infants.

evidence.title: Structure of BT_3984, a member of the SusD/RagB family of nutrient-binding molecules
evidence.study_population: Structural biology of Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (human gut isolate)
evidence.relevance: Confirms the annotation context: PF07980 SusD/RagB is a large family of outer-membrane nutrient(glycan)-binding lipoproteins in gut Bacteroidota, many in PULs of unknown specificity - explains the 'function unknown' annotation and why the family is not diet-source specific.

evidence.title: Metagenome-derived SusD-homologs affiliated with Bacteroidota bind to synthetic polymers
evidence.study_population: Environmental/metagenomic SusD-homolog survey with recombinant protein assays
evidence.relevance: Documents the phylogenetic breadth and Bacteroidota affiliation of SusD/RagB homologs, indicating that abundance of this orthologous group in metagenomes is dominated by Bacteroidota community share rather than by a specific dietary protein source.

contradicting_evidence: No study reports ENOG410XR0J in the opposite (meat-associated) direction either, so this is not scored -1; however the supporting logic is undercut by two observations found in search: (1) in the meat vs. dairy RCT itself the meat arm showed the increase in community richness and in butyric acid, and the only significant between-group genus effect was Akkermansia (Verrucomicrobiota, which lacks SusD/RagB PUL systems); (2) adult diet-microbiome literature retrieved in search repeatedly links Bacteroides dominance to animal-protein/fat-rich intake (and lower Bacteroides in diets free of meat), which would predict Bacteroidota-encoded SusD/RagB genes to be higher in the meat arm. Evidence is therefore mixed rather than clearly directional.

caveats: ENOG410XR0J is an unnamed, function-unknown orthologous group within a very large, taxonomically broad protein family (PF07980 SusD/RagB); literature searches cannot resolve individual eggNOG OG identifiers, so absence of direct evidence partly reflects annotation granularity rather than biological implausibility. Because RagB/SusD gene abundance is expected to scale with Bacteroidota relative abundance, any observed dairy-vs-meat difference in this feature may be a proxy for compositional differences (e.g., Bacteroides/Phocaeicola share) rather than a specific dairy-glycan (lactose, milk oligosaccharide, or dairy-matrix polysaccharide) utilization function; strain-level PUL specificity would need to be shown. Also note that dairy foods contain little complex polysaccharide, so a dairy-driven increase in a PUL substrate-binding protein family is not mechanistically obvious and should be interpreted cautiously. Finally, one key corroborating statement (dairy-associated longitudinal Bacteroides increase) came from a systematic review rather than from the primary report's own between-group test.
